attributes.subject: monopsony
attributes.name: mechanism

value.value: In labour markets, employers can have wage-setting power when workers have limited outside options.

attributes.sourceText: Manning (2021), Monopsony in Labor Markets: A Review; Azar and Marinescu (2024), Monopsony Power in the Labor Market: From Theory to Policy.

attributes.subject: monopsony
attributes.name: mechanism

value.value: This power can arise from employer concentration, job differentiation, and search frictions that make switching jobs costly.

attributes.sourceText: Manning (2021), Monopsony in Labor Markets: A Review; Azar and Marinescu (2024), Monopsony Power in the Labor Market: From Theory to Policy.

attributes.subject: monopsony
attributes.name: example

value.value: a rural town dominated by one hospital may leave nurses with few realistic alternative employers.

attributes.sourceText: Illustrative example based on labour-market mechanisms reviewed by Manning (2021) and Azar and Marinescu (2024).

attributes.subject: monopsony
attributes.name: example

value.value: a worker facing costly relocation or a restrictive non-compete may have limited ability to switch employers even when several employers exist.

attributes.sourceText: Illustrative example based on labour-market mechanisms reviewed by Manning (2021) and Azar and Marinescu (2024).
